analysis.one_liner: Requires every electric utility to offer community solar so renters can buy solar power without rooftop panels.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in the Senate and referred to the Energy and Natural Resources Committee, where it has sat with no cosponsors and no action since June 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require nearly every electric utility to offer a "community solar" program — a shared solar project that any customer, including renters and low-income households who cannot put panels on their own roof, can subscribe to and use to lower their electric bill. It would also direct the Energy Department to help states, tribes, and businesses set these programs up and to open existing federal energy financing to them. It has not moved since being referred to committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Renters, apartment dwellers, and low- and moderate-income households who cannot install rooftop solar would gain a way to buy solar power through a shared local project and see it credited on their utility bills. Solar developers and installers gain a nationwide market, since every electric utility would have to offer a community solar program open to all its ratepayers. States, local and Tribal governments would get federal technical help and financing tools to build programs.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Renters and low-income households without rooftop solar

how_it_helps.text: It amends federal utility law (PURPA) to require each electric utility to offer a community solar program open to all ratepayers, including low-income ratepayers, so renters and others without suitable rooftops can subscribe and offset their electric bills with solar power.

It directs the Energy Department to help states, local and Tribal governments design affordable rate structures, provide technical assistance, and use National Laboratories to help private entities finance and operate community solar projects.

It expands existing DOE grant, loan, and financing programs to cover community solar, and lengthens the allowed term for federal utility-service contracts to 30 years to make long-term solar agreements possible.

analysis.who_pays: Electric utilities would bear the cost of setting up and running community solar programs, and some of that cost could be recovered through rates paid by all customers. The Energy Department and National Laboratories would take on new program, data, and technical-assistance work paid for by taxpayers.

drawbacks.text: The bill mandates that every non-Tribal electric utility offer a community solar program with 'equitable and demonstrable access' for all ratepayers — a compliance cost that utilities would likely pass through to ratepayers, including those who never subscribe.

The bill requires states and nonregulated utilities to hold proceedings and make determinations within two years, with sanctions under PURPA for noncompliance — a federal preemption of state energy regulatory choices that some states may view as unwarranted.

The benefits of community solar subscriptions depend on rate design and sunlight, and the bill lets the program be implemented through utility-owned or third-party facilities, so realized bill savings for subscribers could be modest or uneven depending on how each utility structures its program.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: On its face the bill offers real benefits — cheaper clean energy access for renters and low-income households — at a modest, distributed cost spread across utility ratepayers and financed in part by federal programs. The honest caveats are that it is an unfunded mandate on utilities (some cost will show up in bills or grid investment), that solar benefits vary by location and rate design, and that a one-size federal standard may fit poorly in states with different market structures. None of these drawbacks outweighs the benefit for the households it targets, but the bill is entirely prospective: as of now it has no cosponsors and has not moved, so no one has gained or lost anything.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was read in the Senate and referred to the Energy and Natural Resources Committee, where it has sat without a hearing or cosponsors since June 2025.

narrative.text: Senator Ben Ray Luján introduced the Community Solar Consumer Choice Act of 2025 on June 26, 2025.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Energy and Natural Resources, which is the only action recorded.
No senator has cosponsored the bill.
The bill has not received a committee hearing, a markup, or a floor vote in the Senate.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, no one has gained or lost anything concrete; electric utilities and the solar industry simply face no new federal mandate. If the bill dies quietly, utilities avoid a new obligation and renters without rooftop solar keep none of its promised savings.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one yet; the bill sits untouched in committee

for.name: Sen. Ben Ray Luján
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the Energy and Natural Resources Committee.

sides.party_line_note: The bill has no cosponsors and no votes, so no partisan pattern has formed yet.

industries.note: Utilities are required to offer community solar programs open to all ratepayers and bear the setup and administration costs, but they (or third parties they host) can own the facilities and earn from them. The bill requires a mechanism to mitigate market concentration.

industries.industry: Solar developers and community solar companies
industries.note: A federal mandate that every utility offer a community solar program creates a nationwide market for third-party community solar development, financing, and subscription management.

industries.industry: Low- and moderate-income households without rooftop solar access
industries.note: Renters, apartment dwellers, and shaded-roof homeowners gain a way to buy solar power and offset bills without installing panels.

analysis.trajectory: The bill has no cosponsors and no committee activity since referral in June 2025. Most single-sponsor energy bills referred to committee without cosponsors never receive a hearing or vote, so its most likely path is to die in committee at the end of the 119th Congress unless the committee takes it up or it picks up bipartisan cosponsors.
